title: 06. Distributed Systems & Consistency: Split Brain Problem
summary: Split brain is the failure mode where a network partition causes two or more subsets of nodes to each believe they are the active leader (or primary), independently accepting conflicting writes that diverge the dataset;…
objectives: Define split brain precisely. What are its necessary and sufficient conditions?
Explain why a majority quorum prevents split brain during a partition.
What is a fencing token, and why is it necessary in addition to quorum-based election?
What is STONITH, and when is it preferred over software fencing?

sections.title: Explanation
sections.body:
> **In one line:** Split brain is the failure mode where a network partition causes two or more subsets of nodes to each believe they are the active leader (or primary), independently accepting conflicting writes that diverge the dataset; mitigations include **quorum-based fencing**, **STONITH** (Shoot The Other Node In The Head), **witness nodes**, and **lease revocation** with fencing tokens.

Split brain is the most dangerous failure mode in a distributed system. It occurs when a network partition divides the cluster into two or more isolated subsets, and each subset — unable to see the others — concludes that the others have failed and elects its own leader. Now there are two (or more) leaders, each accepting writes to the same logical data, and the writes are mutually inconsistent. When the partition heals, the system must somehow reconcile two divergent histories, and any choice it makes will lose data from one side. This is the nightmare scenario for any system that claims strong consistency: not just unavailability, but silent data corruption. The CAP theorem tells us we cannot have both availability and consistency during a partition, so the safe choice is to sacrifice availability — exactly one side should remain writable, and the other should refuse writes. The mechanisms that enforce this choice are the subject of split-brain prevention.

The root cause is asymmetric information. During a partition, each side sees half the cluster "missing" but cannot distinguish a network failure (the missing nodes are healthy but unreachable) from a node failure (the missing nodes have crashed). A naive failover protocol — "if I cannot reach the leader, elect a new one" — will trigger both sides to elect their own leaders, because neither side can reach the other. The fix is to require a quorum for leadership: a node can become leader only if it can prove that a majority of the cluster supports it. If a partition splits 3 nodes from 2 in a 5-node cluster, only the 3-node side can reach majority quorum; the 2-node side cannot, and must refuse to elect a leader, becoming unavailable rather than risking divergence. This is the fundamental mechanism underlying Raft, Paxos, and Zab. The architect's first line of defense against split brain is always: require a majority quorum for any leadership change.

Quorums alone are not quite sufficient, because of a subtle race. Even with majority-based leader election, the old leader may not immediately know it has been deposed. It may be paused (GC, slow disk), partitioned, or simply slow to process the message that a new leader has taken over. During this window, the old leader continues to accept writes and may even commit some (if it had a quorum before the partition, its local state still says "I am leader"). When the partition heals, these stale writes can corrupt the new leader's state. The fix is **fencing** (also called **fencing tokens** or **epoch numbers**): every leader is assigned a monotonically increasing token, and every write carries it. Storage systems reject writes with stale tokens, so even if an old leader sends a write after the new leader has taken over, the storage sees the stale token and refuses. Fencing is the second line of defense and is essential: leader election alone does not prevent split brain — leader election combined with fencing does. HDFS, Kafka (KRaft), GFS, ZooKeeper, and Spanner all use fencing tokens.

The third mechanism is **STONITH** (Shoot The Other Node In The Head), a hard-power-off approach used in high-availability clusters like Linux-HA and Pacemaker. When a node is suspected of being a stale leader, the cluster instructs a hardware device (an IPMI board, a networked PDU, or a cloud provider's instance-stop API) to forcefully power off the suspected node. STONITH is brutal but effective: by physically removing the node, it eliminates any possibility of further writes. STONITH is used when software fencing is insufficient — for example, with shared storage where multiple writers can corrupt the filesystem at the block level. The trade-off is operational complexity: STONITH requires correctly configured power-control devices, and a misconfiguration can power off nodes unnecessarily. Modern cloud-native systems prefer fencing tokens over STONITH because they achieve safety without hardware dependencies, but STONITH remains the gold standard for shared-storage HA clusters.

The fourth mechanism is the **witness node** (or **tiebreaker**), used to break ties in even-sized clusters. A 4-node cluster that partitions 2-2 cannot reach majority on either side, leading to full unavailability — the "double-failure" scenario. A witness is a non-data-bearing third node (often in a third location) that participates only in voting. With 4 data nodes plus 1 witness (5 voters), a 2-2 partition is resolved by the witness: the side that can reach the witness has 3 votes (majority), and the other side has 2 (minority, must refuse writes). The witness is cheap to run because it stores no data, only participates in elections. SQL Server AlwaysOn, MongoDB elections, and GlusterFS all use witness nodes. The trade-off is that the witness must be in a third failure domain — if it is colocated with one side, it does not break the tie. The architect must place the witness carefully, typically in a third AZ or third region, with reliable network to both data-bearing sites.

Real-world split-brain incidents have shaped the industry. Elasticsearch before 7.x was notorious for split-brain during network blips: a delayed heartbeat could cause a node to elect itself as master, accepting writes that conflicted with the real master's writes, requiring painful manual reconciliation after heal. Elasticsearch 7+ requires a quorum of master-eligible nodes and uses term-based fencing. MongoDB replica sets use election terms and a writeConcern-majority mechanism that prevents stale primaries from committing. Redis Sentinel has known split-brain edge cases; Redis 6+'s Raft-based Redis Cluster is the recommended path for systems needing correctness. HDFS NameNode HA uses a combination of quorum (ZooKeeper-based) and fencing. The lesson across all these systems is the same: split brain is prevented by the combination of (1) quorum-based leadership, (2) fencing tokens on every write, and (3) operational procedures to handle the rare cases where both fail. The architect's responsibility is to ensure all three layers are in place, because any one alone is insufficient.

sections.title: Visual Explanation
sections.body:
### Mermaid Diagram
```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant A as Node A (leader, term=2)
    participant B as Node B
    participant C as Node C
    participant S as Shared Storage

    Note over A,S: Network partitions: A isolated from B,C
    Note over B,C: B and C elect new leader (term=3)
    B->>S: write(x=2, term=3)  -> ACCEPTED (newer term)
    Note over A: A still thinks it is leader (term=2)
    A->>S: write(x=1, term=2)  -> REJECTED (stale term, fencing)
    Note over A: A receives notice of term=3, steps down
    Note over S: Data is consistent: x=2 wins
```

### ASCII Diagram
```
   before partition:  +---+   +---+   +---+
                      | A |   | B |   | C |    (A is leader, term=2)
                      +---+   +---+   +---+

   partition:    +---+           +---+   +---+
                 | A |  X  X  X  | B |---| C |   (A isolated)
                 +---+           +---+   +---+
                                   B,C quorum=2 -> elect B (term=3)
                                   B writes x=2 to storage (term=3)
                                   storage ACCEPTS (term=3 > 2)

   A (still term=2) writes x=1 to storage (term=2)
                                   storage REJECTS (term=2 < 3)  -> FENCING

   heal: A receives AppendEntries(term=3) -> steps down
         data: x=2 (consistent)
```

### Walkthrough
1. A 3-node cluster is partitioned: node A is isolated from nodes B and C. A was the leader with term=2.
2. B and C form a quorum (2 of 3) and elect B as the new leader with term=3. B writes `x=2` to storage, which accepts it (term=3 is the highest it has seen).
3. A, still believing it is leader, attempts to write `x=1` with term=2. The storage sees term=2 < term=3 and rejects the write (fencing). When the partition heals, A receives B's higher-term message and steps down, leaving the data consistent at `x=2`.

sections.title: Code
sections.body:
```python
import time

class Node:
    """A node in a cluster that may become a stale leader."""
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name
        self.term = 0
        self.is_leader = False
        self.partitioned_from = set()   # peers this node cannot reach
        self.local_writes = []          # (key, value, term)

    def become_leader(self, term):
        self.term = term
        self.is_leader = True
        print(f"  [{self.name}] became LEADER (term={term})")

    def write(self, key, value, storage):
        if not self.is_leader:
            print(f"  [{self.name}] not leader, write rejected locally")
            return False
        entry = (key, value, self.term)
        self.local_writes.append(entry)
        # Storage enforces fencing: rejects writes with stale terms.
        ok = storage.apply(key, value, self.term, self.name)
        return ok

class Storage:
    """Shared storage with fencing-token protection."""
    def __init__(self):
        self.data = {}
        self.highest_term = 0
        self.history = []

    def apply(self, key, value, term, writer):
        if term < self.highest_term:
            print(f"  [STORAGE] REJECT {key}={value} (term={term}) "
                  f"from {writer}: stale (highest={self.highest_term}) <-- FENCING")
            return False
        if term > self.highest_term:
            self.highest_term = term
        self.data[key] = value
        self.history.append((key, value, term, writer))
        print(f"  [STORAGE] ACCEPT {key}={value} (term={term}) from {writer}")
        return True

# Simulate split-brain with fencing
storage = Storage()
A, B, C = Node("A"), Node("B"), Node("C")

# Initial: A is leader, term=1
A.become_leader(1)
A.write("x", 1, storage)
print()

# Network partition: A isolated from B, C
print("-- partition: A isolated from {B, C} --")
A.partitioned_from = {"B", "C"}
# B and C form majority quorum, elect B as new leader, term=2
B.become_leader(2)
B.write("x", 2, storage)              # accepted (term=2 > 1)
print()

# Stale leader A tries to write -- FENCED
print("-- stale leader A attempts write --")
A.write("x", 99, storage)             # rejected by fencing
print()

# Without fencing: show divergence (commented out for safety)
print("-- (without fencing, A's x=99 would have corrupted storage) --")
print(f"  final storage state: {storage.data}  (consistent: x=2)")
print(f"  history: {storage.history}")
```

quiz.question: Explain why a majority quorum prevents split brain during a partition.
options: This is the classic Sentinel split-brain scenario. Detection: monitor both Redis instances with INFO replication; if both report role:master, you have split brain.
This is a classic GC-induced split-brain scenario, and HDFS has explicit defenses.
Three problems. First, the database is a single point of failure: if the database is unreachable, no leader can be elected, and the entire system becomes unavailable.
The fundamental insight is the pigeonhole principle: in a cluster of N nodes, two disjoint subsets of size > N/2 cannot exist, because their combined size would exceed N.
quiz.explanation: The fundamental insight is the pigeonhole principle: in a cluster of N nodes, two disjoint subsets of size > N/2 cannot exist, because their combined size would exceed N. So if a leader must be elected by a strict majority (> N/2 votes), at most one leader can be elected at any time — two disjoint majorities are arithmetically impossible.
